prompt: Plain documentary photograph, 4:5 portrait, of one ancient til laurel (Ocotea foetens) in the laurisilva cloud forest at Fanal, Madeira, Portugal, at the rim of the plateau above the Ribeira da Janela valley. The tree stands large on the left side of the frame, its trunk at least a third of the frame width. Its age-mark is the shape of the trunk itself: long ago the tree was blown over, and the massive lower trunk lies almost horizontal along the top of a big moss-covered dark basalt boulder for about two metres, roots torn up on its left end now re-gripping the rock and the moss, then the trunk bends upward at a near right angle, an elbow, and rises vertically through the left of the frame. This ground-hugging L is the first thing the eye lands on. Every root visibly enters thick moss cushions over the basalt or the dark reddish-brown wet earth; fallen laurel leaves and hand-sized ferns lie at the base for scale. Bark: dark brown, deeply furrowed laurel bark patched with green moss, pale grey-green lichen and small clinging ferns, the furrows twisting around the elbow, not tiled. The top edge of the frame cuts just after the first great limbs leave the upright trunk, one sinuous limb sweeping out horizontally to the upper right, dense clusters of deep green glossless oval laurel leaves on it; the crown carries on out of frame. On the right of the frame, beyond the boulder, the ground falls away: valley mist fills the Ribeira da Janela valley and forested ridges of laurel recede into it, two or three planes, each paler grey than the last, the nearest showing dim rounded grey-green laurel crowns, the farthest a faint grey line. Mist sits behind and around the tree only; the laurel is fully sharp, full-colour and unveiled. Light: soft overcast inside cloud, fog brighter in the upper-left corner where a high sun is hidden; the left flank of the trunk and the top of the horizontal section take the light, the right flank drops half a stop into soft shade with deeper green moss; no cast shadows, no sun, no beams. The top edge of the frame cuts these three leaders soon after they leave the trunk, with flat scale-leaf sprays of yellow-green cypress foliage on them; the crown carries on out of frame.
